p.b:
Black clouds, come dancing, come dancing this way,

Pour on the smiling earth your watery spray;

Feed the tiny saplings, quench their thirst today,

Bring to the farmer's face a smile, I pray.

Out came the moon in the courtyard of night,

A heap of stars followed, all twinkling bright.

He looked at his face in the mirror of lakes,

And dozed among crows like a drunkard late.

The weavers of the town weave cotton threads all day,

Their hands may tire but never does their spirit give way.

Into every warp and weft they pour their heart's own song,

See the shining cloth emerge where patient hands belong.

Scientists tell us that every third bite of food we eat exists because of a pollinator's work. A honeybee moves from flower to flower collecting nectar, and the pollen grains stuck to its legs reach the next flower, helping fruits to form. If bees disappear, half our plates would go empty. Puja asked in class, 'How can we protect bees?' The teacher suggested planting flowering pots on terraces, using fewer insect-killing sprays, and never breaking beehives. The following week, the class created a 'Pollinators' Corner' in the park, where the hum of bees can now be heard all day.

Do not pluck me, gardener, let me on the branch remain,

Let me smile my fill and drink the morning sun again.

Plucked and packed inside your basket, I shall fade alone,

On the branch I shall become the whole garden's tone.

The first ray of morning reached the sparrow's nest,

And wiped away the shadow-drowsy night's dark vest.

The lotus bloomed at every step, the butterfly took wing,

Scattering colours from her tiny petals of spring.

In Manasi's school there is a tradition during the midday meal - every child puts one full bite from his or her plate into a long common plate. Today Shankar, who had been unwell since morning and whose plate was empty, sat nervously. Manasi placed two pooris from her own plate into the common one. One by one, every child's hand carried a bite up to that long plate. When Shankar saw the plate placed before him, his eyes welled up. The cook smiled, 'Child, this school does not serve food alone; it distributes values.'

p.d: गद्यांश: The Doll in the Courtyard
p.b: In my grandmother's courtyard lay an old doll - broken arm, faded colours and one eye missing. Mother told me the doll had been hers when she was a child. She would play with it, scold it and tell it stories. I tied the doll's broken arm with a strip of cloth and made it a bed out of a matchbox. Grandmother laughed and said, 'It is easy to throw away old things; true love lies in mending them.' That evening, listening to the story of the doll's 'wedding', I learnt that love is not in shine but in staying together.

The first time Ali entered the school library, his heart beat faster. Hundreds of books stood in rows on the shelves. The librarian pointed to a corner - 'the picture-story shelf'. Ali picked up a book with a blue cover; its pages carried pictures of the Indus Valley. As he read, he began to wander through the streets of Mohenjodaro. When the bell rang, he was startled - he had been lost inside the book. The librarian smiled and said, 'A good book is a travel ticket; without paying a fare you can journey anywhere.' Ali got his library card made the same day.

My grandmother owns an old cloth bag. It keeps dry fruits given by neighbours, samples of her embroidery, and a few letters. Whenever someone falls ill, grandmother plucks neem leaves from the courtyard, brews a bitter drink, and applies a turmeric paste from her bag. One day I asked her, 'Grandma, who gives you all these things?' She said, 'Child, I served people; what fills this bag is their returned love.' That day I understood that the greatest bank balance in the world is the good we do for others.

Behind our school there is a small garden that the students of Class V look after. On Mondays, it is my turn, along with Salma's, to water the plants. The garden has marigold, rose and mogra plants. In one corner stands an old peepal tree whose branches are always full of chirping sparrows. Our teacher, Sheetal Ma'am, tells us that plants are living things like us; they need sunlight, water and our care. When the first rose bloomed, we did not pluck it. We decided to smile at it every day instead, because a blooming flower belongs to everyone.

Trumpty-trumpty goes the elephant, swinging trunk so slow,

Ears like fans flap to and fro as on his back we go.

Not the jungle's king, we say, but modesty's own crown,

Children love his gentle gait and never wear a frown.

On her way back from the market, Kiran found a purse lying on the road. It contained some money, an old photograph and a receipt. For a moment she thought of keeping it, but then she remembered her mother's words: 'There is no greater charity than returning what belongs to others.' Kiran walked to the shop mentioned on the receipt and handed the purse to the shopkeeper. By afternoon, an old woman arrived at the shop, wiping her tears. The moment she saw the purse, her face lit up. She stroked Kiran's head and said, 'Child, more than the money, it was this photograph that made me weep; it is the only picture of my late husband.' Kiran understood that the true reward of honesty is the blessing it earns.

My book, my dearest friend, gives me the strength of mind,

Fresh tales from every land and every age I find.

When loneliness wraps me close, I turn the pages bright,

And little stories weave for me dreams throughout the night.
